request.job_description: We are hiring an Engineering Manager to lead a team of 6-8 engineers building the core payments platform. You will own delivery, hire and grow engineers, manage performance, partner with product and design on roadmap, and keep the team's technical quality and on-call health strong. Requires 2+ years of people management experience and a track record of shipping reliable backend systems.

transcript.question: Tell me about an engineer you helped grow significantly. What did you do?
transcript.answer: I had a mid-level engineer who wanted to move to senior but kept getting feedback that her designs were too narrow. We agreed on a goal in our first one-on-one: lead one cross-team design within two quarters. I paired her with a staff engineer for design reviews, had her write the RFC for our queue migration, and I stayed out of the room when she presented so she owned it. I gave her written feedback after each review. She was promoted in the next cycle, and two of the teams she worked with asked for her on follow-up projects.

transcript.question: Describe a project that was at risk of slipping. How did you handle it?
transcript.answer: We were rebuilding our billing reconciliation job, planned for 10 weeks, and at week four we were clearly behind because the data volume was three times what we assumed. I cut scope with product by dropping the self-serve report UI and moved two engineers from a lower priority migration onto it. I also started a weekly risk review with a burndown. We shipped in 12 weeks instead of 10, with the core reconciliation intact, and the report UI followed the next quarter. In hindsight I should have load tested earlier, so now we do a data volume check in week one.

transcript.question: Tell me about a time you had to manage out or address an underperforming engineer.
transcript.answer: Yeah, I've dealt with that. Generally I try to give people feedback early and make sure they know where they stand. If things don't improve, I work with HR on the next steps. It's always a hard conversation but I think being honest is the most important thing.

transcript.question: How do you decide when to pay down technical debt versus ship new features? Give an example.
transcript.answer: I try to keep it balanced. We had a flaky payment retry service that caused about five pages a week for on-call. I made the case that it was costing us roughly a day of engineering time every week, plus risk of duplicate charges. I got agreement to allocate 20 percent of one sprint to rewrite it with idempotency keys. Pages dropped to about one a month. I generally reserve around 15 percent of capacity for this kind of work, and I bring the on-call data to planning so it's not just my opinion.

transcript.question: How do you keep product and other stakeholders aligned with your team's work?
transcript.answer: I think communication is really important. I try to keep everyone in the loop and have regular meetings. I send updates when things change. I believe in being transparent so there are no surprises.
